newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Caspian oil row sees new complications.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Caspian oil row sees new complications.

text.p: The future of a billion dollar Caspian oil deal was confused on Friday, with Russia's LUKoil, one of the companies involved, saying it was not clear the project was cancelled.

Less than 24 hours after Turkmenistan said the Kremlin had killed off a preliminary deal between Azerbaijan and Russia to tap a Caspian field, LUKoil said it had received no official word the deal was off.
"We have no official information on the exit of our company from this agreement," LUKOil spokesman Dmitry Dolgov said.

Azerbaijan also weighed in on the biggest crisis yet over ownership of the Caspian's vast reserves, downplaying a fray which could have big implications for U.S., European and Asian companies tapping the region's black gold.
"This is not an instance worth worrying about," Azeri President Haydar Aliyev said of the reported axeing of the deal by Russian President Boris Yeltsin because of problems over who owns the oil.
"I suppose a solution to the situation will be found."

Azerbaijan also said it foresaw a solution to the prickly geopolitical squabble, which involves a field with 50-80 million tonnes of oil in a sea where the total reserves may be second only to those of the Middle East.
At dispute is an accord between Azerbaijan and two Russian oil firms to develop a $1 billion oilfield in the Caspian.

LUKoil, Russia's largest oil company, and Russian state-owned oil holding company Rosneft signed a preliminary accord last month to develop the field, which the Azeris call Kyapaz but the Turkmens, who also claim it, call Serdar.
LUKoil, widely acknowledged as Moscow's unofficial ambassador to the Caspian region, is also aggressively expanding in the area, a potentially ambiguous role.

"The agreement bore a preliminary character and concerned general commercial principles," Dolgov said. "It also contained a point saying that work would be carried out depending on how the disagreement is regulated."

The larger issue is how oil worth tens of billions of dollars will be extracted from the Caspian, a body of water bordered by Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan -- all of which claim some of the spoils.

Russia and Iran say the Caspian is a salt lake whose oil resources are common property to be developed jointly by the five. The rest have argued it is a sea to be divided into sectors, which each country having its own slice.
Russia is struggling to reassert control over oil which it owned in the Soviet era but which is now partly the domain of the former Soviet republics.
Turkmenistan has added to the brew by saying part of the sector which Azerbaijan claims, including the disputed oil field, was really Turkmenistan's. Azerbaijan did not disagree.
"Azerbaijan has never denied that Kyapaz is an interstitial field, since it is located on the border between the Azeri and Turkmen sectors of the sea," Aliyev said.
Azerbaijan's prime minister, Artur Rasizade, called on the Azeris, Russians and Turkmens to tap the field jointly.
